previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: The patient, a male with HLA-B27-positive ankylosing spondylitis, hypertension, asthma, obstructive sleep apnea, and depression, was admitted for acute worsening of mid-back and bilateral SI joint pain that began suddenly the night prior. He reported a fever of 102°F several days before admission but was afebrile during hospitalization. Labs showed mildly elevated inflammatory markers without leukocytosis. An X-ray of the cervical and thoracic spine showed mild degenerative changes but no fracture or ankylosis. Pain was managed with increased hydromorphone and addition of tizanidine for muscle spasms. The patient declined earlier rheumatology follow-up and MRI/CT evaluation. He improved symptomatically and was discharged home with instructions to monitor for worsening pain, fever, or neurological symptoms, and to follow up with his primary care provider.
problems: Ankylosing spondylitis of unspecified sites in spine
Major depressive disorder, single episode, unspecified

biologics due to significant history of infections), asthma, 
OSA, and hypertension, who presents with AS flare of R SI joint 
and R hip pain. On ongoing self-initiated prednisone taper for 
flare. Transitioned to oral basal and breakthrough pain 
management with good effect. Notably improved with pain and

#ACUTE-ON-CHRONIC DORSALGIA: 
#ANKYLOSING SPONDYLITIS: 
Presented to the hospital after unable to manage flare at home 
with increased hydromorphone and self-initiated prednisone 
taper. Of note, has been off of biologics for last several 
months due to own concerns that they were diminishing his 
quality of life by causing more frequent, intolerable 
infections, and that these infections were causing flares. He 
has seen several Rheumatologists and Infectious Disease 
specialists who have reinforced the safety and relatively lower 
risk of biologic treatment with infectious prophylaxis versus 
untreated disease.
 
At presentation, he was given two doses of ketorolac and 
prednisone for pain control. Over the course of his 
hospitalization, we consulted Rheumatology, Chronic Pain, and 
Orthopedics. With Rheumatology, we continued prednisone taper, 
to end ___. We again reinforced the importance of long-term 
treatment and discussed his poor prognosis overall with 
untreated disease. Pain helped guide our management of his 
narcotics: he was initially continued on his regimen of oral 
hydromorphone with IV for breakthrough, and was transitioned to 
PCA on ___, tapered down ___ and discontinued ___ am. Over 
this time, he was transitioned to long-acting Oxycontin for 
basal pain control, with oxycodone ___ put on for breakthrough 
___. 
 
Ortho was consulted for concern that there may be an effusion in 
his hip limiting his mobility and increasing the duration of 
this flare. Per their evaluation, there was no effusion and no 
intervention was indicated.
 
On day of discharge, he is able to ambulate without mobility 
aides and reports greater pain control and ability to sleep 
through the night.
 
TRANSITIONAL ISSUES:
=======================================
- Further pain management contingent on ability to follow up 
with Pain clinic, as below
- Ongoing concern that underlying ankylosing spondylitis remains 
untreated and is progressing past the point of symptomatic 
management

Dear Mr. ___,

It was a pleasure taking care of you at ___. Please see below

WHY WAS I IN THE HOSPITAL?
You came to the hospital with pain in your sacroiliac joint and 
right hip, concerning for an ankylosing spondylitis flare. You 
had started oral prednisone and increasing your narcotic pain 
management at home for this concern, but were unable to manage 
it from home.

WHAT HAPPENED IN THE HOSPITAL?
While at ___, you met with the Rheumatology, Chronic Pain 
Service, and Orthopedics teams. The Rheumatology team helped 
manage your prednisone taper, as below. The Chronic Pain Service 
helped to manage your oral and IV narcotic medications. The 
Orthopedics team assessed you for concern that there may be an 
effusion in your hip, and determined that no radiologic or 
surgical intervention was indicated as you demonstrated no 
symptoms or signs concerning for infection. In addition, we 
continued to monitor your pain and mobility while you were here.

We remained concerned that while your pain improved with this 
care, your underlying illness remains untreated and has become 
more difficult to manage with pain control and intermittent 
medication trials. We encourage you to discuss options for 
long-term treatment with your outpatient providers.

rheumatologist, and the pain management service as below.
